faqs.a: A CSS background pattern is a repeating design built entirely from CSS gradients — radial, linear, conic, or repeating — instead of an image file. Because the browser tiles the gradient mathematically, the pattern stays sharp at any size and costs almost nothing in page weight.
faqs.q: What is a CSS background pattern?

faqs.a: Yes. The patterns this tool generates use standard gradients (radial-gradient, linear-gradient, conic-gradient, repeating-linear-gradient) that have been supported in all modern browsers for years, including Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge. No vendor prefixes are needed.
faqs.q: Do these patterns work in all browsers?

faqs.a: In most cases you cannot stack a pattern over a photo with a single background, because background-image layers replace each other. But you can layer gradients: put the pattern gradient first and the photo URL second in a comma-separated background-image list, and make the pattern semi-transparent so the photo shows through.
faqs.q: Can I combine a pattern with a background image?

faqs.a: For the best performance, keep the tile size small (16–48px) and prefer simple two-stop gradients. Patterns are painted by the GPU and are generally cheap, but very large tiles with many gradient layers can slow down low-end phones when scrolling.
faqs.q: Do CSS patterns slow down my page?

faqs.a: Yes — every pattern here is plain CSS, so you can drop the output into a Tailwind project via arbitrary values (for example bg-[radial-gradient(...)]), a styled component, or a utility class in your stylesheet. For repeated use, save it as a CSS class or variable.
faqs.q: Can I use these with Tailwind or styled-components?

faqs.a: The quickest way is the pattern itself: set the shape color to transparent-ish and let the page background show through. Or use background-blend-mode: overlay on the patterned element so its color mixes with whatever sits behind it.
faqs.q: How do I make a pattern blend with the section behind it?

howTo: Pick one of the eight pattern styles: dots, grid, diagonal stripes, horizontal stripes, checkerboard, cross, zigzag, or waves.
Choose the base color and the pattern color with the color pickers.
Drag the tile-size slider to make the pattern denser or sparser; the preview updates live.
Copy the generated CSS class and paste it into your stylesheet.
Rename the .my-pattern class to whatever fits your project, and apply it to any element.
keyFacts: CSS patterns are made from gradients, not images: radial-gradient draws dots and circles, linear-gradient draws lines and stripes, and conic-gradient draws checkerboards.
The browser tiles the gradient automatically using background-size, so a few lines of CSS can fill an entire page with a seamless pattern.
Because gradients are resolution-independent, CSS patterns stay perfectly sharp on retina and 4K displays without extra assets.
A typical pattern declaration is under 300 bytes — orders of magnitude smaller than a PNG or SVG doing the same job.
Multiple gradient layers can be comma-separated in one background-image, which is how zigzag, cross, and wave patterns are built.
background-size controls the tile: smaller tiles make the pattern denser, larger tiles make it bolder and sparser.

limitations: Estimates only in the sense of rendering: very old browsers (Internet Explorer) do not support conic-gradient or multiple backgrounds well.
Complex multi-layer patterns can be harder to read in code than a simple class name — add a comment when you paste them.
Patterns are decorative; keep contrast ratios accessible when text sits on top of a patterned background.
The zigzag and wave patterns use fixed math that looks best at tile sizes that divide evenly.
